CEE 1001.d: Students are exposed to a cross section of topics in computer and electrical engineering disciplines to assist them with their education and career choices. Task-exposure research consistently marks manual laboratory work as low-exposure, and the jagged-frontier caution applies acutely at the bench, where trusting a model's expected value over a real measurement produces errors. Foundational role in the accredited sequence reinforces the course's place. The rating stays Low. Even as analysis and lab-report drafting automate, the psychomotor and verification skills this laboratory builds resist substitution, and diffusion of AI into hands-on instruction lags its diffusion into desk work.

A decade out, AI is a capable lab assistant, interpreting instrument data and drafting reports, and some measurement may be automated through instrumented benches. CEE 2145.d: Students study the theory, modeling and application of semiconductor based electronic circuits. The devices include: diodes, MOSFET transistors, voltage regulators and operational amplifiers.

r: The course builds skills to analyze and design logic circuits using Boolean algebra, Karnaugh maps, and truth tables, and introduces computer architecture, number systems, codes, combinational circuits, logic gates, flip-flops, and memory. Logic minimization and design entry are highly exposed, indeed logic synthesis has been automated for decades, and observed usage confirms Computer and Mathematical work as the largest category models touch. But CEE 2310 is critical foundational scaffolding for the ABET-relevant computer-engineering sequence, prerequisite to Digital Systems II, Signals and Systems, and embedded design, so students must understand the architecture well enough to specify and verify what synthesis tools and AI produce. At twenty-four months the instrumental need to build digital-logic and architecture fundamentals is not eroded: AI can minimize a function, but the course grounds the substrate later required courses assume. Foundational role and ABET context hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will fluently derive minimized logic, generate combinational and sequential designs, and explain architecture, sharpening the question of why students learn to do it by hand. But the jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant: an engineer who cannot read a truth table, trace a flip-flop, or reason about a memory map cannot verify AI-generated logic, and that verification competence is exactly what the foundations build. Foundational scaffolding for the entire computer-engineering sequence caps the erosion at Medium regardless of how automatable entry-level logic design becomes. The rating rises to Medium. The instrumental case shifts from deriving logic to specifying and validating it, a Medium, not a High, because the foundational knowledge remains required for that oversight, and because task-exposure research pairs high programming exposure with a persistent need for the underlying reasoning to catch confident errors.

A decade out, AI generates and optimizes digital logic and architectural blocks routinely, and the design-it-by-hand rationale is substantially eroded. But the conceptual foundation, Boolean reasoning, state machines, memory and architecture, remains necessary to specify systems, catch non-obvious logic errors, and verify AI output, and it scaffolds the whole computer-engineering major, while ABET content structures persist. The rating holds Medium, explicitly capped by foundational role from going High. The wide uncertainty concerns how digital logic is taught when tools synthesize it, not whether the fundamentals remain instrumentally necessary as verification and specification knowledge; the evidence says they do. Confidence is medium because digital design is unusually amenable to automation, making the precise long-run balance between AI synthesis and residual human oversight harder to call than for more embodied courses, though the foundational cap reliably prevents full elimination.
CEE 2310.d: Students will develop the skills necessary to analyze and design logic circuits using Boolean algebra, Karnaugh maps and truth tables. They will also develop an understanding of the basic concepts of computer architecture. In addition, this course covers number systems, operation and codes. Combinational digital circuits are also studied. The use of basic logic gates, Flip-flops, memory, integrated circuits, as well as the design of digital systems will be covered in detail.

r: This introductory programming course teaches C and C++ for engineering problem-solving and introduces shell scripting. Coding is among the most-exposed tasks in the entire evidence base: it is the single largest observed-usage category, task-exposure research associates programming strongly positively with exposure, and controlled studies show large developer speedups, GitHub Copilot raising task speed by roughly 56 percent. That pushes exposure high, and AI already writes competent introductory C and C++. But CEE 2350 is critical foundational scaffolding, prerequisite to embedded design and pervasive across the computer-engineering curriculum, which caps the rating at Medium even at twenty-four months: students cannot meaningfully specify, supervise, or debug AI-generated engineering code without understanding programming fundamentals. The instrumental case for writing the code yourself is already partly eroded, but the substrate role, and the ability to verify AI output, keeps the course necessary. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI coding assistants will handle most routine C, C++, and shell implementation for engineering tasks, and the write-it-yourself rationale weakens further. Yet the jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant: engineers who cannot read, verify, and debug AI-generated code, especially memory-unsafe C on constrained hardware, produce unreliable and unsafe systems, and that verification competence is exactly what these foundations build. As load-bearing scaffolding for embedded and later computing courses, the rating is capped at Medium regardless of how automatable entry-level coding becomes. The instrumental case shifts decisively from writing code to specifying and validating it, a Medium rather than a High because the foundational knowledge remains required for oversight. Productivity gains skew to lower-skill users, meaning novices gain most from AI, but that uplift presupposes the reading fluency this course establishes.

A decade out, AI generates most engineering software, and the developer role centers on specification, architecture, and verification. Introductory programming's execution rationale is substantially eroded, but the conceptual foundation, control flow, data structures, memory, and how C maps to hardware, remains necessary to do the higher-order work, catch the model's non-obvious failures on embedded targets, and scaffold the whole major. The rating holds Medium, explicitly capped by foundational role from going High. The wide uncertainty concerns how programming is taught when AI writes the code, not whether computational fundamentals remain instrumentally necessary; the evidence, and the safety cost of unverified low-level code, says they do, increasingly as verification knowledge. This mirrors the introductory-computing anchor: the highest task-exposure in the evidence base, held to Medium by an unambiguous foundational-scaffolding role across the computing curriculum.
CEE 2350.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. Introductory C/C++ and shell-script programming course whose outcome is writing routine code to solve engineering problems. Stanford's August 2026 payroll update places software developers and computer programmers in the most AI-exposed occupations, where employment of 22-to-25-year-olds is 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put computer programmers at -7.3%. Both are descriptive signals, not proof that AI caused the decline. No rating changed, because institutional lock-in and foundational-course caps already binds.
CEE 2350.d: This is an introductory level programming course using C and C++ languages for engineering students. Methods for solving computer engineering problems using the two programming languages are studied. The fundamentals of shell scripts are also introduced.

CEE 3330.d: This course is a continuation of CEE 2310. It covers the analysis and design of sequential (counters and shift registers) logic systems. Programmable Logic Devices (PLD) and associated Computer Aided Design (CAD) software are used to implement digital circuits by using the schematic design entry method. Johnson counter and Ring counter are studied. The general methods of analysis and design for Finite State Machine (FSM) is also introduced.

CEE 3400.d: Students are introduced to the basic concepts of signals and system modeling. The students develop and understand time- domain and frequency-domain analysis of both continuous and discrete systems and signals.

CEE 3620.d: This course is an introduction to communication systems. Topics include: information theory, channel capacity, A/D and D/A techniques, modulation (AM, FM, and digital), noise sources, quantization, and transmission lines including Smith Charts.

r: The internship provides supervised, practical, hands-on experience in a professional computer- or electrical-engineering setting, arranged through the Classroom to Career hub. Its instrumental content is the situated workplace experience itself, working within a real engineering team, navigating professional norms, and applying knowledge to live problems under supervision, which is inherently embodied and present-tense.
